What it does

Recon takes two lists that should agree, such as invoices and bank receipts, and works out which rows explain each other. It reports what matched, by which rule and how confidently, what is still open on each side, and how old the open receivables are.

How it works

Each side is mapped to four fields: date, amount, reference and counterparty. References are normalised (upper case, punctuation removed, filler words such as “INV” or “payment for” dropped). Then five passes run in order; a row used by one pass is not reused by a later one.

  1. Exact. Same normalised reference and the same amount to the cent.
  2. Tolerance and timing. Amount within the tolerance and dates within the window. Closest date wins; confidence falls as the gap grows.
  3. Fuzzy reference. Amount within tolerance and a Jaro-Winkler similarity between the references above the threshold. Jaro-Winkler rewards shared characters and a shared prefix, which suits invoice numbers with a typo.
  4. One-to-many and many-to-one. For an open row, the engine looks for two to four open rows on the other side (same counterparty when both are known, within the group window) whose amounts sum to it, using a bounded subset-sum search over at most 14 candidates. That cap is what keeps the worst case small.
  5. Duplicates. Rows with the same reference, amount, date and counterparty on the same side are flagged. One copy can still match; the other is listed under Duplicates.

Ageing takes the unmatched side-A rows and buckets them by days outstanding at the “as of” date: 0–30, 31–60, 61–90 and 90+.

Amount buckets are indexed by rounded value, so each lookup touches only neighbouring buckets instead of the whole other side. On the synthetic sample scaled to 10,000 rows per side the engine finishes in well under a second in Node; the target in the brief was 5 seconds.

Why I built it

Limits

  • Greedy matching: each pass takes the best candidate it sees and moves on. It does not search for a globally optimal assignment.
  • Rule 4 looks for groups of up to four rows among the 14 nearest candidates. A payment covering twenty invoices will not be found.
  • Only the first sheet of a workbook is read, and the first row must be the header.
  • Everything lives in memory in one tab. Very large files (hundreds of thousands of rows) may run out of memory on a phone.
